design_detail: Single-author narrative review of what is known about MDMA and body temperature in people, written in 2011: placebo-controlled laboratory studies (Table 1), studies of people at dance clubs and parties (Table 2), hospital case reports and series of severe overheating, thermal self-ratings (how hot people say they feel), proposed mechanisms of heat production and loss, and behavioural and environmental co-stressors (Table 3). Animal work is cited only as background. Method as stated: an extensive personal collection of MDMA papers was scrutinised and then a PubMed search was run with thermal key words; no search string, dates, selection rules, number of papers screened or appraisal method are given (Section 1, 3rd paragraph, p. 2).
can_establish: What one author found when he gathered the human temperature studies up to mid-2011: the size and spread of the temperature rises reported in laboratory and in party settings, examples of severe overheating in hospital series, how much people differ in how hot they say they feel, and a list of hypotheses about what makes overheating worse, with the review's own statement of which are untested.
cannot_establish: The size of the average temperature effect of MDMA (the figures are unweighted averages of studies that used different thermometers, doses and comparisons); whether dancing, crowding, a hot room, too little or too much water, other drugs or low thermal awareness raise the risk of severe overheating (the review itself calls most of these untested or very limited); what share of people who take MDMA overheat; or anything about prevention (the review's treatment passages are not used here).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Evidence base as listed in the tables: laboratory studies of 4 to 16 volunteers; party and club studies of 11 to 41 people; one Internet survey of over 200; hospital series of 48 and 332 admissions; individual case reports (Tables 1 and 2, p. 3; Sections 3-5, pp. 4-6).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated. Selection began from the author's personal collection and a PubMed search with unstated key words (Section 1, 3rd paragraph, p. 2).
sample.selection_effects: The author's own work supplies three of the five party studies in Table 2 (Parrott and Young, 2005; Parrott et al., 2007b; Parrott et al., 2008) and the Internet survey of over 200 people; the party studies are small convenience samples at clubs and parties (11 to 41 people each), and one source is a conference abstract (Tancer et al., 2003) and another is cited as a single page (Morefield et al., 2009). Cases from hospitals show the people who became ill, not how many took MDMA and did not.

exposure.measurement: Varies by cited study. Laboratory: dose given by the study team. Parties: MDMA confirmed by blood (Irvine et al., 2006; Morefield et al., 2009) or saliva (Parrott et al., 2008) in some studies, by self-report in others; doses unknown (Sections 2-3, pp. 2-5).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, as summarized: oral doses of 0.25 to 2.0 mg/kg, or 75, 100 or 125 mg, in laboratory studies; in party studies, self-obtained tablets, 1 to 5 in one study and on average 6 over a night in another (Section 2, pp. 2-4; Section 3, pp. 4-5).
exposure.polysubstance: Laboratory studies: MDMA alone. Party studies: methamphetamine was found in 41% and cannabis in 33% of one sample, other drugs were taken occasionally in another, and one study asked people not to take other stimulants (Section 3, pp. 4-5). The author suggests stimulants may add to body temperature and cannabis may lower it, on very limited data (Table 3; Section 8).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable to a review; in two party studies the same people were also studied on a weekend without MDMA (Section 3, p. 4).

comparison.controls: Laboratory: placebo sessions in the same people, except the first pilot study (Grob et al., 1996), whose text describes baseline sessions only. Parties: no comparison at all in one study; people who had never taken ecstasy at the same club in one; the same people on a weekend without MDMA in two; the person's own pre-drug baseline in one (Sections 2-3, pp. 2-5).
comparison.matching: Varies. The club comparison of people who took ecstasy that evening with people who had never taken it and with former takers is between people; the two weekend studies are within person.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Parties: dancing, room temperature, crowding, fluid intake, sleep and the time of night are not controlled; the review notes that without a control condition the normal fall of body temperature during the night is uncontrolled (Section 3, Irvine paragraph, p. 4).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not controlled in the party studies.

outcomes.instruments: Oral, axillary, tympanic (ear), rectal and ingested radio-telemetry core temperature and skin temperature in the laboratory; ear or oral temperature at parties; self-rated feeling hot, hot and cold flushes and sweating by questionnaire, interview and Internet survey (Tables 1 and 2, p. 3; Section 5, p. 6).
outcomes.validity_norms: Different body sites do not give the same temperature; the author notes, quoting an animal study, that ear temperature can be lower than and independent of blood temperature (Section 8, p. 8).
outcomes.operationalization: Peak change in temperature against placebo, baseline or a comparison group. Dose tiers in Table 1 are the unweighted means of the rows within each tier; 'higher dose' means 2.0 mg/kg.

analysis.effect_sizes: As summarized (Tables 1 and 2, p. 3; Sections 2-3). Laboratory peak core temperature change: up to 1.0 mg/kg, from -0.1 to +0.3 degrees Celsius, tier mean +0.1; 1.1-1.9 mg/kg, +0.3 to +0.5, mean +0.4; 2.0 mg/kg, +0.4 to +1.0, mean +0.7 (14 people in two studies by the same three authors, each at two room temperatures). In the two studies that varied room temperature, 18 against 30 degrees: +1.0 and +0.8 (4 people) and +0.4 and +0.6 (10 people). One volunteer in an 8-person study rose 1.9 degrees against a group mean of +0.4. Plasma MDMA and temperature correlated with p<0.0001 in the laboratory (Kolbrich et al., 2008) and r=+0.38, p=0.058 at a party (Irvine et al., 2006). Party studies, peak change: +0.2 (27 people, no control), +1.2 against clubbers who had never taken it (32), +0.3 (12; -0.2 on a weekend without MDMA, +0.15 with), +1.6 (11 people, 6 tablets on average, against a weekend without), +1.1 oral and +1.8 skin (41 people). Thermal self-ratings, Internet survey of over 200: 16% not hot, 41% slightly, 31% moderately, 12% strongly or extremely hot.
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection without a stated search. The review reports small and null results (Grob et al.; Vollenweider et al.; Kolbrich et al.; Irvine et al.), which counts in its favour. Table 3 states that high room temperature was associated with higher core temperature in the laboratory, which the text of the same review does not support.
analysis.power: Not applicable. The review notes where small samples limit a result (14 women in one overview).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In placebo-controlled laboratory studies of 4 to 16 volunteers, core temperature rose on average about 0.1 degrees Celsius at low doses, 0.4 at moderate and 0.7 at 2.0 mg/kg, with one volunteer up 1.9; the two studies that varied room temperature found similar rises at 18 and 30 degrees. At parties, group averages rose between 0.2 and 1.6 degrees in five small studies with different comparisons, the largest (+1.6) in the group that took 6 tablets on average over the night. Severe overheating above 40 degrees is described in hospital series and case reports of people who became ill, with no denominator. How hot people said they felt varied widely (16 in 100 not hot at all). Dancing, crowding, other drugs and thermal awareness as risk factors are hypotheses, and the review says so.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Section 8 state that MDMA is clearly a thermal stressor in people and that its effects were dose related; that real-world variation is possibly due to physical activity, ambient temperature and overcrowding; that moderate hyperthermia can progress to severe hyperpyrexia through a cascade of events; and that low thermal awareness might put people most at risk. The first statement is well supported by the laboratory studies. 'Dose related' is a pattern across studies, not shown within any one study. The cascade and the risk factors are explicitly hypotheses (Section 7, p. 7; Table 3).

timeline.event: Pilot study of six volunteers at four low doses: no significant change in oral temperature (Grob et al., as summarized in this review).
13 volunteers at 1.7 mg/kg: about +0.2 to +0.5 degrees Celsius, not significant; one brief hypertensive crisis (Vollenweider et al., as summarized).
8 men at 75 and 125 mg: peak +0.4 degrees at 2 hours (Mas et al., as summarized).
16 and 14 volunteers at 1.5 mg/kg: +0.3 to +0.4 degrees, significant (Liechti et al., as summarized).
4 volunteers at 2.0 mg/kg at 18 and 30 degrees: +1.0 and +0.8 (Tancer et al., conference abstract, as summarized).

10 volunteers at 2.0 mg/kg at 18 and 30 degrees: +0.4 and +0.6, with delayed onset of sweating (Freedman et al., as summarized); also 32 clubbers who had taken ecstasy, 1.2 degrees above clubbers who had never taken it (Parrott and Young).
27 people at a dance party: +0.2 degrees, no control condition (Irvine et al., as summarized).
8 volunteers: +0.3 to +0.4 degrees, not significant, one person +1.9 (Kolbrich et al., as summarized); 12 clubbers on and off MDMA (Parrott et al.).
41 people at parties, 1 to 5 tablets: +1.1 degrees oral (Morefield et al., conference abstract, as summarized).
166 healthy volunteers in nine controlled studies from one laboratory: highest temperature 39.1 degrees, none above 40

replication.where_it_stands: A rise in core temperature after MDMA at rest has been found by several independent laboratories, in small studies; its average size is a few tenths of a degree at moderate doses. The effects of heat, dancing, crowding and other drugs on that rise have not been tested in people, and the review says so. Severe overheating is known from hospital cases only.

funding.funder: Nothing declared (Role of funding source, p. 8).
funding.affiliations_note: Single author, Department of Psychology, Swansea University; also author of three of the party studies and the Internet survey reviewed here.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review with a stated search and appraisal; person-level data from placebo-controlled studies at several doses read with one thermometer type; controlled human studies that change one factor at a time (room temperature, activity, fluid intake, a second stimulant) within ethical limits; and party studies that follow matched people who did not take MDMA at the same event, with temperature logged at fixed times and the blood level measured.

domains.note: Starts from a personal collection plus a PubMed search with unstated key words; no dates, criteria or count of papers.
Informal appraisal in the text (no control condition, borderline significance, pooled time points, a study left out of Table 1 because it had no placebo) but none that is systematic.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Three of the five party studies in Table 2 and the Internet survey are the author's own.
Untested hypotheses are mostly labelled as such (Table 3; Section 7), but the Table 3 row on room temperature states a laboratory finding that the text does not report.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against
domains.note: Reports null and small results; the cascade of co-stressors rests on animal, survey and case evidence.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3). The review is open about what is untested, but its selection is unsystematic and rests partly on the author's own studies, and one table row contradicts its own text. Use it for the list of studies, the figures it reports for each (cite the primary study where it can be read), and the author's statements of what is untested; do not use it for causes of severe overheating.

key_findings.finding: Method: the author scrutinised a personal collection of MDMA papers and then searched PubMed using thermal key words; laboratory and real-world studies were grouped separately. No search string, dates or selection rules are given.

Placebo-controlled laboratory studies (4 to 16 volunteers each): peak core temperature change by dose tier averaged +0.1 degrees Celsius up to 1.0 mg/kg (rows -0.1 to +0.3), +0.4 at 1.1-1.9 mg/kg (rows +0.3 to +0.5) and +0.7 at 2.0 mg/kg (rows +0.4 to +1.0); the highest tier is 14 people in two studies by the same three authors, each tested at two room temperatures. The tier means are unweighted and use oral, axillary, ear and swallowed sensors.

Room temperature: in the two laboratory studies that tested 18 and 30 degrees Celsius, MDMA raised core temperature by +1.0 and +0.8 (4 people) and +0.4 and +0.6 (10 people, swallowed sensor); the review reads the overall effects as broadly similar in both conditions. MDMA also raised metabolic rate and delayed the start of sweating.
key_findings.locator: Section 2, paragraphs beginning 'Tancer et al. (2003) tested four volunteers' (p. 2) and 'The next study comprised the most comprehensive' (p. 3); Section 6, 1st-2nd paragraphs (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Variation between people: in an 8-person laboratory study the group mean rise was +0.4 degrees but one volunteer rose +1.9; blood MDMA correlated with the temperature rise (p<0.0001). At a dance party the two of 27 people with the highest blood levels (0.77 and 0.84 mg/l) had the largest rises (+1.0 and +1.6), with a borderline correlation overall (r=+0.38, p=0.058).
key_findings.locator: Section 2, last paragraph (pp. 3-4); Section 3, 1st paragraph (p. 4); Section 8, 1st paragraph (p. 7); Table 3, row 'MDMA plasma level' (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Party and club studies, peak temperature change: +0.2 degrees (27 people, no control), +1.2 against clubbers who had never taken it (32 people), +0.3 (12 people, on against off MDMA), +1.6 (11 people, 6 tablets on average over the night, against a weekend without), +1.1 oral and +1.8 skin (41 people, 1 to 5 tablets; 25% had blood levels the paper reports as in the toxic to lethal range by forensic guidelines, and the high doses were generally well tolerated, with enjoyment).

Hospital series and cases of severe overheating: a woman at 41.6 degrees Celsius two hours after taking MDMA powder found to be pure with no other substance, who survived (a friend who took the same powder had no reaction); a 16-year-old who died after one tablet, her second time, with blood MDMA 0.424 mg/l and no other drug; she was one of seven deaths with temperatures of 40-43 degrees in United Kingdom poisons-unit enquiries of 1990-91, where blood MDMA ranged from 0.11 to 1.26 mg/l, which the original authors said did not reflect high dose levels, and where the most severe cases showed overheating, widespread clotting, muscle breakdown and acute kidney failure; 332 emergency admissions to one London hospital over three years, with core temperatures on arrival from 34.1 to 41.6 degrees.
key_findings.locator: Section 4, 2nd-3rd paragraphs (p. 5); 5th paragraph beginning 'Following the early case studies' (p. 5); paragraph beginning 'Halpern et al. (2011) described' (pp. 5-6)

key_findings.finding: Thermal self-ratings: in an Internet survey of over 200 people 16% said they did not feel hot on MDMA, 41% slightly, 31% moderately and 12% strongly or extremely; in the laboratory study with a warm room there was no significant overall drug effect on the ratings, though feeling warm rose 2 to 4 hours after MDMA. One woman at a club shivered and felt cold while her temperature was unchanged. The author suggests, as a hypothesis for study, that people with low thermal awareness might be most at risk of severe overheating because they may not cool down.
key_findings.locator: Section 5, 1st-2nd paragraphs (p. 6); Section 7, paragraph beginning 'An important question' (p. 7); Section 8, 2nd paragraph (p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Factors the review lists as possibly raising thermal stress: higher single doses or repeated binge doses, prolonged dancing, crowded and hot clubs, other stimulants, low thermal awareness; and as lowering it: rests and cooler places, possibly cannabis. In its own Table 3 it notes that crowding and loud music have not been investigated, that data on dancing and on other drugs are very limited, and that age, gender, genetics, hydration and personality need study. Hydration is called a contributory factor in animals that needs testing in people.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, rows 'Dance clubs: prolonged dancing' to 'Other factors' (p. 4); Section 7, paragraph beginning 'An important question' (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: In one sentence the review says that low blood sodium arises when a person drinks too much water as a reaction against feeling too hot, and describes it as dilution of sodium and potassium; no data are given.
key_findings.locator: Section 4, paragraph beginning 'to 1.26 mg/l' (right column, 1st paragraph)

key_findings.finding: Overview: the author concludes that MDMA is clearly a thermal stressor in people; laboratory studies found a dose-related rise (minimal at low doses, about +0.4 at moderate and +0.7 at higher doses), and party studies a wider spread, possibly due to dosing or bingeing, lifetime use, dancing, environment and other drugs.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3, row 'Ambient temperature', says that in the laboratory high ambient temperature was associated with higher core body temperature, with complex combined effects. The text reports the opposite for the two studies that varied it: nearly identical core temperatures under both conditions (Tancer et al.: +1.0 at 18 and +0.8 at 30 degrees) and effects broadly similar (Freedman et al.: +0.4 and +0.6).
reporting_issues.consequence: The table row overstates a laboratory effect of room temperature; the text is the better guide, and it rests on 14 people.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives 16 volunteers for Liechti et al. (2000b); the text says 14.
reporting_issues.consequence: A small inconsistency in a sample size.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists ear (tympanic) temperature for Tancer et al. (2003), but the text says core temperature was measured with rectal probes.
reporting_issues.consequence: The body site of the highest-dose rows is unclear; it matters because sites differ in accuracy.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 is headed as an overview of placebo-controlled studies, but the text describes the first study (Grob et al., 1996) as comparing post-drug sessions with baseline sessions, and the dose tiers mix doses given as mg/kg and as fixed mg, with oral, axillary, ear and swallowed sensors.
reporting_issues.consequence: The tier means, which carry the 'dose related' conclusion, are unweighted averages of unlike measurements.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 puts three different things under one heading, peak temperature change: change from the person's own baseline (Irvine et al.; Morefield et al.), difference from people who had never taken ecstasy at the same club (Parrott and Young), and difference between a weekend with and a weekend without MDMA (Parrott et al., 2007b and 2008). The +0.3 for Parrott et al. (2008) is not stated in the text, which gives -0.2 on the weekend without MDMA, +0.15 with it, and a borderline difference (p=0.08).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures in Table 2 cannot be ranked against one another; the spread from +0.2 to +1.6 reflects different comparisons as well as different parties.

reporting_issues.issue: The two largest party-based rises in ear temperature (+1.6 and +1.2) come from the review author's own small studies (11 and 32 people), one against a non-using comparison group and one against a weekend without MDMA; the next (+1.1 oral, +1.8 skin) is cited as a single page (Neuropsychobiology 60:216), which suggests an abstract. Tancer et al. (2003) is a conference abstract.
reporting_issues.consequence: Peak party temperatures rest on small, partly unreviewed reports.

reporting_issues.issue: The severity bands from Grunau et al. are printed with reversed signs: severe as '<40.0' and extreme as '<42.0' degrees Celsius, where above is meant.
reporting_issues.consequence: A printing error; the thresholds are above 40 and above 42 degrees.

reporting_issues.issue: Hyponatraemia is described as dilution of sodium and potassium; the condition is a low blood sodium. The sentence cites a hospital series and gives no data.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cannot be used for anything about low sodium; the primary papers should be read instead.

reporting_issues.issue: No search string, dates, databases other than PubMed, inclusion rules or count of papers screened are reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Completeness cannot be judged; a study that did not find an effect may be missing.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1-9 (PDFs/MDMA/Parrott_2012_MDMAAndTemperature.pdf), full text including Tables 1-3, funding and the reference list (read for the conference abstracts); Tables 1 and 2 and the Irvine paragraph were checked against rendered images of printed pages 3 and 4, and the Grunau thresholds against a rendered image of page 6.
